q4_0_vs_q4_1_anomaly.summary: Q4_0 has a 10% byte-size edge per element, but on gfx906 decode (batch=1) it loses to Q4_1 by ~2.8% in this codebase. Mechanism is BOTH (a) a kernel-ecosystem maturity asymmetry on the flambeau side AND (b) a hardware truth that flips the textbook expectation: gfx906 decode is latency-bound, not HBM-bandwidth-bound.

byte_economics.q4_0_block: 2 B (half scale) + 16 B (4-bit qs nibbles) = 18 B / 32 elems = 0.5625 B/elem (symmetric quant: y = scale · (q − 8))
byte_economics.q4_1_block: 2 B (half scale) + 2 B (half min) + 16 B (4-bit qs nibbles) = 20 B / 32 elems = 0.625 B/elem (affine quant: y = scale · q + min)

q4_0_vs_q4_1_anomaly.naive_expectation: If MMVQ at decode were HBM-bound, Q4_0 should be ~10% faster than Q4_1. Even my earlier diagnosis in `qwen36_27b_q4_0_tp2_decode.json` claimed 'large-n_rows calls are HBM-bound (ffn_gate at 20 MB/call ~30 µs at 700 GB/s)' — that calc was right for the GEMM proxy but wrong for the actual gfx906 schedule.
q4_0_vs_q4_1_anomaly.actual_hardware_behaviour: Web-corroborated finding: gfx906 at batch=1 (decode) sits at ~10% effective HBM bandwidth utilisation — the kernel is LATENCY-bound, not bandwidth-bound. The MI50 has wide HBM (1024-bit, ~1 TB/s peak) but the at-batch=1 single-row MMVQ schedule can't keep the memory pipe full because each output row's cooperative-thread-block work doesn't issue enough concurrent loads to amortise the HBM latency. Result: per-block compute + scheduler ILP dominates, and the 10% byte advantage of Q4_0 doesn't show up.
q4_0_vs_q4_1_anomaly.measured_on_this_rig: Qwen3.5-27B Q4_0 26.70 tok/s vs Q4_1 27.46 tok/s (+2.8% for Q4_1). 27B-Q8_0 24.09 tok/s — also confirms decode is NOT bandwidth-bound: Q8_0 reads ~1.42x the bytes of Q4_1 (34 B vs 20 B per 32 elems) but runs only ~12% slower, not 1.42x slower. The flat-ish curve across Q4/Q8 is the latency-bound signature.

q4_1_variants_in_dispatch_table: mmvq_q4_1_t128 (128 threads, half-warp DPP-reduce — V2.2.b production winner)
q4_0_variants_in_dispatch_table: mmvq_q4_0 (256 threads, DP4A — only production variant)
kernel_ecosystem_asymmetry_in_flambeau.consequence: Q4_1 picks the t128 schedule (2 wave64s/CU, 2 blocks per CU at typical grids) which packs more in-flight work per CU on the latency-bound MMVQ. Q4_0 is stuck on 256-thread (4 wave64s/CU = 1 block per CU at occupancy ceiling), throwing away the latency-hiding opportunity its smaller weights should enable.

q4_0_vs_q4_1_anomaly.consequence_for_this_session: Cycle 1 (mmvq_q4_0_gate_up_dp4a) and cycle 3 (mmvq_q4_0_kv_f16dst_dp4a) both use 256 threads/block (mirrored the Q8_0 gate+up template). They saved real launch overhead, but they're stuck on the same latency-throwing-away schedule. A future cycle could write `mmvq_q4_0_t128` + `mmvq_q4_0_gate_up_t128_dp4a` to realise Q4_0's silicon advantage on this latency-bound regime.
q4_0_vs_q4_1_anomaly.estimated_ceiling_with_t128: Closing the current 2.8% Q4_1-win plus capturing the 10% byte-size edge on Q4_0 would put Qwen3.5-27B-Q4_0 at ~30 tok/s on TP w=2 (vs today's 26.70). Still latency-bound — hitting that ceiling requires the same kernel maturity Q4_1 already has.

Biggest winner Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_S MoE (62.26 → 67.08 = +7.7%) — many small Q4_0 expert weight reads benefit most from the 2-blocks-per-CU schedule. Q4_1 + Q8_0 unaffected (different kernels).

key_design_choices_seen_in_their_q4_0_ke: __launch_bounds__(64, 1) — 64 threads/block (one wave64), even thinner than our cycle-5 t128
2 rows per block: row = blockIdx.x * 2 + (lane_id / 32), grid = (n_rows + 1) / 2
Half-warp per row: 32 lanes loop through blocks_per_row with stride 32 (each thread handles entire Q4_0 blocks)
8 DP4A per Q4_0 block per thread (full block in one thread vs our 4-lanes-per-block × 2 DP4A pattern)
Per-thread loads 16 B of Q4_0 weight + 32 B of Q8_1 activation per block iter
Half-warp (32-lane) DPP reduce at the end (warp_reduce_sum<32>)
Q4_0 dequant: `d4 * (sumi * d8 - 8 * s8)` where `s8 = bq8->ds.y` is the precomputed Q8_1 sum-correction
external_corroboration.implication_for_our_cycle_6: Their schedule is even thinner than ours (64t vs our 128t) — 2× more concurrent blocks per CU = more aggressive latency hiding. They also fold full Q4_0 blocks per thread (8 DP4A/block instead of our 2), which trades thread parallelism for per-thread compute density. Worth A/B'ing as cycle 6: a 64-thread-half-warp-per-row Q4_0 MMVQ + fused gate+up variant.
